meeting was posted on September 8, 2026, at 4:39 PM. This meeting is being recorded 
and is live on S.A.T.V. and Zoom unless technological issues interrupt the

Councilor Smith  moved to dispense with the reading of the record of the previous

President Merkl requested that everyone please rise to recite the Pledge of Allegiance. 
 
Salem City Council Land Acknowledgement 
 
 
 
The Salem City Council honors that this land is Naumkeag, or fishing place, where 
generations of Naumkeag people from the Pawtucket band of the Massachusett Tribe 
lived and passed through for centuries.  
 
We acknowledge that this is unceded Indigenous land and also acknowledge the 
Massachusett Tribe, who continue to honor and hold this land into the present.  
 
Salem’s City Council is committed to having ongoing meaningful dialogue with the 
indigenous peoples who have presence in Salem in order to dismantle the legacies of 
oppression and inequities that persist today.  
PUBLIC TESTIMONY 
 
Prior to Public Comment Councillor Holappa moved that the Council extend public testimony to 
17 minutes to give each person one full minute to speak. Seconded by Councillor Varela. By a 
Roll Call Vote of 10 Yea, 0 Nay, 1 Absent the matter carried. Councillor Prosniewski was 
recorded as absent.
2 
CITY OF SALEM 
SEPTEMBER 10, 2026 
REGULAR MEETING 
 
• Linda Szpak: Opposed changing the Salem city seal, arguing that the seal represents the 
city’s history and should not be erased or rewritten. She said she finds the existing image 
beautiful and questioned why a depiction of a person from the Spice Islands should be 
considered unacceptable, comparing it to other historical aspects of Salem that remain 
part of the city’s identity. 
• Jeff Cohen: Supported changing the city seal and urged the Council to adopt the 
recommendations of the seal task force. He also suggested that restrictions on speed 
bikes should apply to all city parks, not just the Common, citing concerns about people 
traveling at high speeds in parks such as Palmer Cove. 
• Flora Tonthat: Supported changing the seal and argued that civil rights and racial 
justice issues should not be decided through a popular vote that could allow a majority to 
impose its will on a small minority. She cited Salem’s racial demographics and said 
retaining the seal would allow the larger white population to override concerns raised by 
the AAPI community and other vulnerable groups. 
• Jaya Savita: Supported replacing the seal, saying the imagery does not represent 
Salem’s history or contemporary community and perpetuates racial stereotypes. She 
emphasized Salem’s historical connections to Asia while arguing that those connections 
can be recognized without caricaturing Asian people and said changing the seal would 
reflect Salem’s history of evolving with the times. 
• Brett Seferian: Supported changing the seal and challenged arguments that the existing 
image should be preserved without imposing contemporary views on it. He argued that 
the seal was created by white Salem merchants rather than Asian people and said 
historical evidence shows Asian communities faced discrimination in Salem. He 
emphasized the principle of “nothing about uswithout us,” arguing that non-AAPI 
residents should not speak for the AAPI community about how the imagery is perceived. 
• Nicole Eichfret: Supported changing the seal, emphasizing that Asian Americans and 
their ancestors should not be represented through caricatures. She said Salem can 
celebrate its maritime and Asian trade history in ways that do not reduce Asian 
communities to stereotypical imagery. She also connected the issue to the City Council’s 
land acknowledgment and the broader principle of meaningful dialogue with 
communities represented by civic symbols. 
• Dr. Aditi Ahlawat Seferian: Supported changing the seal and spoke about her 
experience as a Salem AAPI resident and former member of the seal task force. She 
described facing fear of harassment and backlash while advocating for the change and 
said the existing imagery is particularly troubling in the current political climate. She 
urged the Council to act according to its conscience rather than choosing the safer or 
more popular position. 
• Isabell Leshko: Supported replacing the seal, citing support from local and state civil 
rights and community organizations, including the Massachusetts AAPI Commission, 
NAACP North Shore branch, and Salem’s Racial Equity Commission. She argued that 
retaining the seal would disregard the perspectives of people who experience racism and 
would prioritize one interpretation of Salem’s history over creating an inclusive civic 
identity.
3 
CITY OF SALEM 
SEPTEMBER 10, 2026 
REGULAR MEETING 
 
• Professor Thomas Green: Supported replacing the seal, explaining that a city seal is a 
public statement about a community’s values rather than merely a historical image. He 
said the existing seal does not represent the values of some Salem residents and 
suggested preserving it in a permanent historical display while allowing the community 
to develop a new seal reflecting shared contemporary values. 
• Jennifer Winsor: Supported retiring the current seal, describing its depiction of an 
Asian person as stereotypical and racist. She said Salem’s maritime history could be 
represented in a more respectful and contemporary way and noted that other 
municipalities have replaced symbols viewed as marginalizing. 
• Steve Kapantis: Opposed changing the imagery, questioning where the process of 
removing historically problematic symbols would end. He compared the Latin on 
Salem’s flag to the Roman Empire’s history of conquest and the dove to Judeo-Christian 
symbolism, arguing that applying similar standards could eventually require removing 
multiple elements of the flag and seal.

MEAN-TESTED CITIZEN PROPERTY TAX EXEMPTIONS (SENIOR TAX 
EXEMPTION) 
 
The following order from the Mayor was adopted 
Ordered: 
The City of Salem shall continue to provide Mean-Tested Citizen Property Tax 
Exemptions, also known as the senior tax exemption program, for an additional 
three years as provide in Chapter 228 of the Massachusetts Acts of 2020, 
concluding on December 31, 2029. 
 
Councillor Davis explained that Salem adopted the STEP (Senior Tax Exemption Program) in 
2020. He noted that the program uses a percentage of the state Circuit Breaker income tax credit 
to determine the exemption amount, allowing more Salem seniors to qualify for property-tax 
relief. He also highlighted that the program’s income thresholds adjust annually with inflation 
and that it does not impose asset restrictions, allowing seniors who own valuable homes but 
have limited incomes to qualify. 
 
Councillor Flynn expressed support for the STEP program and emphasized its importance for 
seniors struggling with basic expenses such as food, heating, and other bills. He said the 
Council should help protect seniors from being forced to leave their homes and praised the city 
for maintaining the program, expressing hope that it will continue in the future.

Section 1. Chapter 12, Section 12-164 General permit fees are hereby

Councillor Sydoriak moves to refer this to the committee on Ordinance, Licenses and

electrical permit fee structure, which had not been updated in about two 
decades, and bring the fees more in line with those of nearby communities 
while remaining below some communities such as Lynn. He referred the matter 
to the Ordinances, Licenses & Legal Affairs Committee to clarify how the 
electrical permit fees interact with building permit fees and ensure there are no 
unintended effects. He also noted that the updated fees would help cover the 
city’s administrative costs for processing permits. 
 
Councillor Varela thanked Councillor Sydoriak for referring the proposal to 
committee and said he wanted a thorough review of how the fee changes would 
affect the overall permitting process. He noted that permit fees had also been 
changed the previous year and said the Council should discuss the proposal 
with the Building Commissioner to understand its practical impact on people 
applying for permits before adopting the changes.

The next amendment struck the language establishing a specific Memorial

3. Expand the exemption to all city departments

4. Retain the emergency exemption 
 
The ordinance included a provision allowing the mayor, fire chief, or 
designee to issue a temporary exemption from the prohibition for 
emergencies, major storms, or public safety needs. Although the chair 
questioned whether the provision was still necessary after exempting all city 
departments, Councillor King argued that it could apply to emergencies 
involving private property or situations where residents could provide gas-
powered equipment to assist the Fire Department. The provision was retained 
and the matter carries. 
 
5. Remove city departments from the 2030 compliance requirement 
 
The ordinance amendment stated that residential property owners, 
commercial leaf blower operators, and all city departments would have to 
comply with the prohibition by January 1, 2030. Councillor Smith moved

discarding functioning blowers. Councillor Holappa also discussed concerns 
about the shorter timeline. The roll-call vote was 2–8, so the amendment

The committee then voted on a separate motion to remove the tiered 
compliance dates for residential property owners, commercial operators, 
and city departments. The chair stated that the motion would strike all 
three dates. The matter carries. 
8. Add outreach and notification requirements 
 
The final amendment added an outreach and notification section. It directed 
the city's sustainability and building departments to conduct outreach to 
inform commercial landscaping companies, retailers within a 10-mile radius,

requirements and timelines. The effective-date section was also struck. The 
matter carries.
